stories.headline: NIAS chief: response times 'unacceptable and intolerable'
stories.body: NIAS chief executive Jenny Keane told Stormont's health committee that Category 1 calls are averaging about 11 minutes (target 8) and Category 2 about 64 minutes (target 18). She apologised to the patients affected.
stories.why: Evidence on the record from the trust's own chief, a week after NI's handover figures.

stories.headline: WMAS budgets for 380,000 hours lost at hospitals
stories.body: West Midlands Ambulance Service told its board that rising fuel prices will add about £1m to costs this year. It is budgeting for crews to lose 380,000 hours outside hospitals by the end of the financial year, and is holding vacancies open to stay on budget.
stories.why: Lost hours mean fewer crews free to respond, and held vacancies matter to job-seekers.

stories.headline: JRCALC Clinical Update 3:26 adds Stroke and TIA guideline
stories.body: The latest JRCALC update adds a new Stroke and Transient Ischaemic Attack guideline, updated medicines monographs and other revisions. It's live in the JRCALC Plus app now.
stories.why: Worth a read before your next shift or placement so you know what has changed.
keywords: joint royal colleges ambulance liaison committee

stories.headline: NEAS joins aircraft emergency exercise at Newcastle
stories.body: NEAS crews, fire, police and the British Red Cross practised a full-scale response to an aircraft emergency at Newcastle Airport, using a Boeing 737 and 150 volunteer 'passengers' to treat many simulated casualties at once.
stories.why: Major incident triage and multi-agency working, rehearsed in realistic conditions.

stories.headline: Prince William visits SCAS staff wellbeing programme
stories.body: The Prince of Wales visited South Central Ambulance Service's Wexham Resource Centre in Slough to learn about its Workforce Wellbeing Programme, backed by a £250k NHS Charities Together grant. An early project is trauma-awareness training for student paramedics.
stories.why: Investment in staff wellbeing, with support starting before students reach placement.

stories.headline: CQC upgrades EEAST from 'inadequate' to 'good'
stories.body: The CQC has raised EEAST's urgent and emergency care rating to 'good', with its control rooms also rated good, after improvements in call handling, dispatch, staffing, training and response times. Handover delays remain the biggest risk.
stories.why: A big turnaround for crews and control staff, with demand up almost a fifth since 2022.

stories.headline: NEAS fastest-responding service in England
stories.body: October NHS England data shows NEAS reached Category 1 patients in an average of 5 min 33 s, inside the 7-minute target and quickest in the country (national average 7:59). It leads every category but, like all services, is still missing the Category 2 target.
stories.why: Shows what's achievable on Cat 1, while Cat 2 remains the national pinch point.

stories.headline: NWAS extends voice note-taking to more crews
stories.body: After an eight-week trial with 40 clinicians found it clinically safe, NWAS is extending ambient voice technology that turns patient conversations into draft clinical notes for crews to check. Nearly 25% of on-the-road staff have signed up.
stories.why: Less time on paperwork, more on patients, but crews still check and own the record.

stories.headline: £648k for paramedic simulation suites in Bedford
stories.body: The University of Bedfordshire has won Office for Students funding for immersive simulation spaces at its Bedford campus for BSc Paramedic Science and nursing students, including emergency-response and paediatric scenarios. They're due to be ready by March 2027.
stories.why: Realistic simulation builds confidence before students face the real thing on placement.

stories.headline: Chest pain pathway sends 86% home same day
stories.body: In Forth Valley, Scottish Ambulance Service clinicians use Consult Connect to speak directly to specialists, and suitable low-risk chest pain patients go straight to a rapid assessment unit, skipping the ED. In year one, 86% went home the same day.
stories.why: Under 1% were readmitted within seven days: alternative pathways working as intended.

stories.headline: Major incident at Manchester's Co-op Live
stories.body: NWAS declared a major incident at 10.25pm on 22 November after a substance, believed to be tear gas, was released near the end of a concert. HART crews attended, more than 50 people were checked and one patient went to Manchester Royal Infirmary.
stories.why: A real-world test of CBRN and major-incident triage, with decontamination done as a precaution.

stories.headline: Over half of north Wales handovers topped 45 minutes
stories.body: 2,028 of 3,800 handovers (53.4%) at Betsi Cadwaladr hospitals went over 45 minutes in October, the worst in Wales, where the overall figure was 34.3%. Welsh Ambulance board papers say the health board is 'not yet progressing' against its plan.
stories.why: Every long handover is a crew held at hospital instead of answering the next 999 call.

stories.headline: LAS newly qualified paramedic jobs close 24 November
stories.body: London Ambulance Service is recruiting newly qualified paramedics for courses starting 15 and 22 February 2027. There is a £2,500 skills incentive for applicants who already hold a C1 licence and a blue-light driving qualification.
stories.why: Final-year students: applications close on 24 November, so don't leave it late.

stories.headline: EEAST video cardiac arrest desk wins HSJ Award
stories.body: EEAST's Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest Desk won the Digitising Patient Care Award at the HSJ Awards on 20 November. Advanced paramedics send callers a secure GoodSAM video link to see the scene and coach bystanders through CPR and defib use.
stories.why: Better bystander CPR before crews arrive gives every patient a stronger chance.

stories.headline: £14m air ambulance base approved in Leicestershire
stories.body: Harborough council approved the Air Ambulance Service's Catthorpe base on 18 November. It will have two helipads, a hangar and training facilities, replacing the base at the now-closed Coventry Airport, and will host the National Children's Air Ambulance.
stories.why: A long-term home for air ambulance crews serving the Midlands and beyond.

stories.headline: LAS declares critical incident as 999 calls surge
stories.body: London Ambulance Service took more than 7,000 calls a day for three days running, higher than most New Year's Eves. Life-threatening breathing emergencies are up almost 20% on last November.
stories.why: Extra crews and phone-based clinicians are being used to reach the sickest patients first.

stories.headline: Hospitals ask EMAS to pause 45-minute handover rule
stories.body: After repeated hospital requests to pause it, EMAS says it is "not assured" the 45-minute release-to-respond limit can be met consistently this winter. AACE says pauses should only happen in exceptional, strictly governed cases.
stories.why: Release-to-respond limits are what get crews back on the road during winter pressure.

stories.headline: NI two-hour handover cap missed 2,000+ times
stories.body: Release to Rescue caps hospital handovers at two hours, but more than 2,000 went over between May and August. That is down from 6,000+ in the same months last year. An RCEM doctor warns it will be 'very challenging' this winter.
stories.why: Progress is real, but winter will test whether the cap holds.

stories.headline: £6m major-incident training suite opens
stories.body: A new Immersive Skills Suite in Gloucestershire, run by the NHS Resilience Emergency Capabilities Unit and hosted by LAS, is open to ambulance services across England. Crews can rehearse terror attacks, chemical incidents, collapses, fires and train crashes.
stories.why: Realistic rehearsal builds confidence for the rare, high-stakes jobs.

stories.headline: Royal College of Paramedics marks 25 years
stories.body: The Prince of Wales, the College's patron, will host frontline paramedics at Windsor Castle on 25 November for its 25th anniversary, including a former Army combat medic and HART members. The College now has more than 21,000 members.
stories.why: A milestone for a profession that has grown a long way in 25 years.

stories.headline: £23m plan to end corridor care in Wales by 2029
stories.body: The Welsh Government's new emergency care plan aims to end A&E corridor care by 2029. It says ambulance handovers averaged 2h24m in 2025-26, adding up to 184,850 lost crew hours.
stories.why: Handover delays keep crews off the road. This plan sets the target to judge progress against.

stories.headline: CQC upgrades SCAS leadership rating
stories.body: The CQC has moved South Central Ambulance Service's leadership rating up from inadequate to requires improvement. Inspectors praised a more stable leadership team, but there is still work to do to reach 'Good'.
stories.why: Stable leadership shapes the culture, support and morale crews feel on the road.

stories.headline: NI health staff to be balloted on strikes over pay
stories.body: Unite will ballot around 4,000 health and social care workers across 10 NHS employers from 23 Nov to 14 Dec. NI staff haven't had the 3.3% 2026-27 rise already paid in England and Wales.
stories.why: Pay parity across the four nations is still unresolved for NI staff.

stories.headline: EEAST adds military co-responders at Northwood
stories.body: Volunteers from all three Armed Forces at Northwood HQ will start answering 999 calls from early December. Existing schemes at five other sites have given 6,000+ hours and helped 2,300+ patients since January.
stories.why: Co-responders can reach patients early and support crews on scene.

stories.headline: NEAS crew based at Durham's Night Safe Hub
stories.body: Until the end of December, a NEAS crew is based at St Nic's Church on Wednesday, Friday and Saturday nights to see people on a night out. The crew still responds to 999 calls when needed.
stories.why: A good model of night-time care that helps keep people out of A&E.

stories.headline: October: a record 28,000 incidents a day
stories.body: NHS England's October figures show a record 28,000 ambulance incidents a day. Category 2 response averaged 32 min 45 s and hospital handovers averaged 32 min 11 s.
stories.why: Winter pressure is building. Expect long waits at handover and stacked calls.

stories.headline: Microsoft outage disrupts NHS email and Teams
stories.body: A global Microsoft outage on 13 November took down Outlook and Teams across the NHS. 999 and 111 call handling and dispatch carried on, but GMB said crews were left with slower manual workarounds.
stories.why: A reminder to know your service's downtime procedures before you need them.

stories.headline: Unite challenges Right Care, Right Person phase two
stories.body: Phase two began on 1 November, moving welfare checks the PSNI used to do to paramedics and GPs. Unite says this puts paramedics at greater risk, following another serious attack on a crew in the Foyle area.
stories.why: Crew safety on welfare calls is now a live issue for NI paramedics.

stories.headline: SECAmb and SCAS sign for shared 999 and ePCR systems
stories.body: The two services, now in a group model, have signed with Cleric for a shared Computer Aided Dispatch and electronic patient care record platform. The Isle of Wight service will use it too.
stories.why: If you work or study in the South East, the ePCR you document on will change.

stories.headline: Shetland's first paramedic retires after 38 years
stories.body: Niall Bristow became the isles' only paramedic in 1992, when ambulances were driven by porters with no medical training. Shetland now has 11 paramedics and 6 technicians covering 16 inhabited islands.
stories.why: A great look at how far the profession has come. Happy retirement, Niall.

stories.headline: 85-year-old waited over 16 hours after a fall
stories.body: MS Paul Davies raised the west Wales case in the Senedd on 10 November and asked for a ministerial statement. Welsh hours lost to handover delays fell from 265,000 to 184,000 last year, but remain over three times the 2016–17 level.
stories.why: Handover delays still hold crews at hospital while older fallers wait at home.

stories.headline: NI ambulance chief: "One attack is one too many"
stories.body: Following the assault at Altnagelvin Hospital, NIAS chief executive Mark Cochrane has appealed for abuse of paramedics to stop. Hundreds of incidents have been recorded this year alone.
stories.why: Violence against crews is still far too common. Report every incident, however minor.

stories.headline: RCEM: fix flow and beds, not just ED funding
stories.body: The Royal College of Emergency Medicine says overcrowding and corridor care stem from a lack of beds and alternatives to admission. About 13,000 beds are taken by patients who don't need to be there.
stories.why: Hospital flow is the root of the handover delays crews face every shift.

stories.headline: HCPC report on regulating advanced practice
stories.body: Commissioned by NHS England, the HCPC and the osteopathy regulator have published findings on how registrants, managers and leaders understand regulation at advanced levels of practice, and where more clarity is needed.
stories.why: Worth a read if advanced paramedic practice is part of your career plans.

stories.headline: NWAS HART paramedic wins treble swimming gold
stories.body: NWAS HART paramedic Carl Barkley won three golds and a silver at the Great British Masters Swimming Championships.
stories.why: A reminder that life outside the job matters. Congratulations, Carl.

stories.headline: Scottish Ambulance Service to take on up to 280 NQPs
stories.body: Backed by £4m of Scottish Government funding, SAS is welcoming up to 280 newly qualified paramedics this year. The Health Secretary met new starters at Livingston on 9 November.
stories.why: A hopeful contrast to the tight NQP job market elsewhere in the UK.

stories.headline: Coroner warns after two women waited 17–24 hours
stories.body: A coroner has sent Prevention of Future Deaths reports to the Welsh Ambulance Service after two women in north Wales fell at home and waited 17 to 24 hours for an ambulance. Hospital handover delays were named as a major factor.
stories.why: Long waits for fallers carry real risk. WAST points to its falls desk and the 45-minute handover target.

stories.headline: Terror response funding falls short of trusts' ask
stories.body: NHS England has set out about £34m to boost ambulance services' terror-response capability, but it appears well short of what trusts asked for. It follows last month's warning that the sector isn't terror-ready.
stories.why: Major-incident readiness depends on kit, training and people on the ground.

stories.headline: JRCALC hypoglycaemia guidance to be reviewed
stories.body: An Essex coroner issued a Prevention of Future Deaths report after a 60-year-old woman treated for severe hypoglycaemia wasn't conveyed and later died. AACE has confirmed the JRCALC hypoglycaemia flowchart is under review.
stories.why: The review includes when patients need hospital. Watch for JRCALC updates.

stories.headline: Dedicated end-of-life ambulance for Bradford and Craven
stories.body: YAS patient transport crews now run a seven-day palliative and end-of-life ambulance between hospital, hospice and home. It builds on a Leeds service that has run for 10 years.
stories.why: Faster discharges at the end of life, and more emergency ambulances free for higher-acuity calls.

stories.headline: Paramedic seriously assaulted at Altnagelvin Hospital
stories.body: A Northern Ireland Ambulance Service paramedic with 37 years' service was attacked by a patient for several minutes during a stretcher-to-chair transfer in Derry on Saturday. Police have identified a suspect.
stories.why: She suffered head, neck, face and hand injuries. Violence against crews remains a real risk, even inside hospital.

stories.headline: CQC finds corridor care at Nottingham's QMC
stories.body: A new CQC report rated urgent and emergency care at Queen's Medical Centre as requires improvement, with patients treated in corridors. One 84-year-old waited nearly 40 minutes to be taken off the ambulance.
stories.why: Handover delays at ED keep crews off the road and away from the next 999 call.

stories.headline: North East teams share major-incident lessons
stories.body: NEAS hosted the North East Specialist Capabilities Conference for ambulance, HART, air ambulance and trauma clinicians. Talks included research on 13,000+ trauma patients and a keynote from the first paramedic on scene at 7/7.
stories.why: Worth following if you're interested in a HART or critical care career.

stories.headline: Survivor's campaign funds 10 public defibs
stories.body: A cardiac arrest survivor worked with London Ambulance Service for 18 months to raise over £21,000 for ten public defibrillators in Queen's Park, Kensal Rise, Carlton Vale and Willesden. Nearly 400 residents have been trained in CPR.
stories.why: Bystander CPR and nearby defibs give crews a better chance when they arrive.

stories.headline: Two-day-old baby saved by dad's CPR and EEAST crew
stories.body: A two-day-old girl stopped breathing at home near Ipswich. Her dad started CPR and a crew including a student paramedic arrived within four minutes, joined by a critical care paramedic. She has now been reunited with the team.
stories.why: Early CPR plus a fast response made the difference, and a proud moment for the student on the crew.

stories.headline: LAS crews speak out on sexual abuse on duty
stories.body: London Ambulance Service has launched the latest phase of its Respect campaign, with a paramedic describing being sexually assaulted on duty. LAS reported 462 sexual-abuse incidents in the year to July 2026.
stories.why: Almost two-thirds of women on ambulances in the NHS Staff Survey report unwanted sexual behaviour from the public.

stories.headline: Roadside blood test flags brain bleeds in minutes
stories.body: East Anglian Air Ambulance's BRAIN-FIRST programme uses a handheld analyser at scene. In its first 65 non-traumatic coma patients it caught every bleed, and it has since been used in more than 200 suspected serious brain-injury cases.
stories.why: Faster diagnosis at scene could help crews get patients to the right hospital first time.

stories.headline: EMAS prepares its first electric ambulances
stories.body: East Midlands Ambulance Service will gradually bring electric ambulances into frontline use from early 2027, under a nationally funded NHS programme. Crews will get specialist training first.
stories.why: The NHS aims for all new ambulances to be zero-emission from 2030, so this is the fleet of the future.

stories.headline: NEAS signs regional anti-racism pledge
stories.body: North East Ambulance Service has signed the Become the Bridge Anti-Racism Pledge, committing to practical action within 12 months to tackle racism in its workplace and in patient care.
stories.why: A fair, inclusive workplace matters for staff wellbeing and retention, and for the care patients receive.

stories.headline: College of Paramedics awards now open
stories.body: Nominations for the Royal College of Paramedics Honours and Awards are open until 12 February 2027. Student members can enter the Carol Furber Award with a reflective case study of up to 1,000 words.
stories.why: A chance to recognise great colleagues. The student winner is published in Paramedic INSIGHT.

stories.headline: Many crews at life-threatening calls lack a paramedic
stories.body: An HSJ analysis found that in large parts of the country, three in 20 ambulances reaching patients with life-threatening emergencies have no paramedic on the crew.
stories.why: It feeds straight into the skill-mix debate and what the paramedic's role on a frontline crew should be.

stories.headline: 21 patients died after heatwave ambulance delays
stories.body: Board papers show 21 patients died after delayed responses from an ambulance service during June's heatwave, when serious calls spiked sharply.
stories.why: Surge planning for extreme weather is a patient safety issue, not just a performance one.

stories.headline: Essex handover delays 'like 291 ambulances off the road'
stories.body: An East of England Ambulance Service report says August's lost handover hours equalled 291 ambulances off the road. Broomfield's average handover rose from about 26 minutes to over 1 hour 12 minutes. NHS England now wants a 45-minute maximum.
stories.why: Every hour held at hospital is an hour a crew can't respond to the next 999 call.

stories.headline: Welsh Ambulance overtime bill tops £109m
stories.body: FOI figures show staff worked nearly 3.9 million paid overtime hours since 2017, costing over £109m. The trust also had the highest sickness absence rate in NHS Wales, 7.7%, in April to June 2026.
stories.why: Heavy overtime and high sickness point to a stretched workforce, a key factor in wellbeing and retention.

stories.headline: SWASFT handles more than 7,000 incidents in a weekend
stories.body: South Western Ambulance Service responded to 3,502 incidents on Saturday and 3,535 on Sunday, around 10% above expected. It blamed seasonal illness, colder weather and hospital handover delays.
stories.why: Winter pressure has arrived early, with Bonfire Night still to come.

stories.headline: PSNI scales back police welfare checks
stories.body: From the start of November, police in Northern Ireland will only do concern-for-welfare checks where there is a risk to life, risk of harm or a crime, under Right Care Right Person. Some 999 calls will be passed to health, social care or other services.
stories.why: Some calls police no longer attend may be passed to health services, which matters for ambulance crews in NI.

stories.headline: National early warning score for children in A&E
stories.body: Emergency departments in England are bringing in a standard Paediatric Early Warning System (PEWS), scoring vital signs so deteriorating children are escalated fast. Any concern from staff, parents or the child triggers an immediate review.
stories.why: Knowing how EDs score and escalate sick children helps make paediatric handovers sharper.

stories.headline: Fuel costs squeeze East of England air ambulances
stories.body: Magpas says fuel costs have left a £50,000 hole in its budget, about 17 missions. East Anglian Air Ambulance expects around £200,000 more a year if prices stay high, while demand is at record levels.
stories.why: Charity-funded air ambulances are a key part of prehospital care, and rising costs put that capacity under pressure.

stories.headline: LAS violence unit backs staff through 640 police cases
stories.body: London Ambulance Service's Violence Reduction Unit helps colleagues report assaults, chase stalled investigations and even get closed cases reopened. Its manager is a former crew member who was once trapped by an aggressive patient.
stories.why: If you're assaulted at work, you shouldn't have to face the reporting process alone.

stories.headline: Visually impaired call handler takes 999 calls at EMAS
stories.body: A 21-year-old with the eye condition Stargardt disease answers 999 calls at East Midlands Ambulance Service using screen-magnifying software, with his guide dog beside him. It's a first for the trust.
stories.why: Other ambulance services have been in touch about opening similar roles to visually impaired people.

stories.headline: WMAS crews lost 32,810 hours outside hospitals
stories.body: West Midlands Ambulance Service told its board that in September only 28.5% of handovers were done within 15 minutes and 22.7% took over an hour. Category 2 response times have improved.
stories.why: Hours at hospital are hours not responding. The trust warned patient harm is "undoubtedly happening".

stories.headline: LAS and EMAS brace for a busy Halloween weekend
stories.body: LAS says Category 1 calls have climbed to around 480 a day, against about 400 on a typical busy day. EMAS is adding extra crews and vehicles after 3,865 calls last Halloween, versus about 3,400 on a normal day.
stories.why: Halloween and Bonfire Night fall within a week of each other, so expect busier shifts across both.

stories.headline: Ambulance CEO warns sector isn't ready for terror attack
stories.body: A chief executive who has led ambulance trusts for 23 years has warned the sector is not "sufficiently trained, equipped, or resourced" to respond to a terrorist attack.
stories.why: Major incident readiness affects every crew. It's worth knowing your trust's plans and your role in them.

stories.headline: Contract to train hundreds of SWASFT support workers
stories.body: Training provider MediPro has won a contract to train hundreds of Level 3 Ambulance Support Worker (Emergency) apprentices for South Western Ambulance Service, starting January 2027.
stories.why: More support workers means more crewing capacity, though some providers have closed amid sector cuts.

stories.headline: Baby born in an ambulance on the A96
stories.body: A Moray mum gave birth in the back of an ambulance between Elgin and Aberdeen, with a paramedic helping. Consultant-led maternity at her local hospital has been downgraded since 2018.
stories.why: Long rural transfers mean emergency birth skills can be needed on any shift.

stories.headline: EEAST reports record 999 demand in September
stories.body: The East of England Ambulance Service took nearly 100,000 999 calls and attended over 84,000 incidents in September, up from about 90,000 calls a year earlier. Crews lost more than 18,000 hours waiting to hand patients over.
stories.why: Rising demand plus handover delays means fewer crews free to respond, and longer waits for patients.

stories.headline: SECAmb pilots live video calls for cardiac arrests
stories.body: Since 26 October, SECAmb critical care paramedics can send callers a secure, unrecorded video link in a suspected cardiac arrest to see the scene, coach bystander CPR and brief crews before arrival. The pilot runs for four weeks.
stories.why: Seeing the scene early could improve bystander CPR. The trust hit its best-ever 30-day survival rate of 17.2% in May.

stories.headline: NEAS trials AI note-taking on crew iPads
stories.body: North East Ambulance Service is running an eight-week trial with 38 staff using ambient voice tech to record, transcribe and summarise patient conversations. Every note is checked by a clinician before it goes on the record.
stories.why: Less time on paperwork could mean more time with patients, but clinicians stay accountable for the record.

stories.headline: LAS signs deal to run its EV charging network
stories.body: As London Ambulance Service grows its electric fleet, Optimo Energy will manage more than 700 charging connectors, linking vehicle telematics and battery data so ambulances are charged and ready between jobs.
stories.why: Electric ambulances are coming, and keeping them charged is now part of keeping crews on the road.

stories.headline: SAS trains for resus in a packed nightclub
stories.body: Scottish Ambulance Service and fire crews ran resuscitation scenarios in an Edinburgh Cowgate bar, with loud music, darkness, haze and bystanders added to practise leading and communicating under pressure.
stories.why: Organiser and paramedic Steve Reiffer called it "stress inoculation": rehearsing chaos so real jobs feel calmer.

stories.headline: UNISON: handover delays harming patients and crews
stories.body: In a UNISON survey of 654 ambulance staff in England, 59% said patients got worse while waiting to be handed over and 7% had cared for someone for 12 hours. 34% are thinking of leaving.
stories.why: Handover delays aren't just a target issue: they affect patient safety and whether colleagues stay.

stories.headline: NWAS renews paramedic apprenticeship with Cumbria
stories.body: A new five-year deal with the University of Cumbria keeps the route open for EMTs to train as paramedics while working. More than 600 NWAS staff have qualified this way since 2021, with teaching now at Lancaster and Liverpool Hope University.
stories.why: Earn-while-you-learn routes widen who can become a paramedic and help grow the workforce.

stories.headline: Some NIAS ambulance defibrillators have faults
stories.body: Some Corpuls3 defibrillators on NIAS double-crewed ambulances have intermittent module connection errors. Backup Zoll AED Pros are being put on board while power boards are replaced. No patient harm has been found.
stories.why: Most faults were caught on daily vehicle checks, a reminder of why those checks matter.

stories.headline: SECAmb plans £24.8m Make Ready Centre in Farnborough
stories.body: Guildford-area crews would start and end shifts at a hub where specialist teams clean and restock vehicles, working from local response posts in between. Tongham and Haslemere stations are under review; no closures have been announced.
stories.why: Make Ready models change how crews start shifts and where they are based day to day.

stories.headline: Scaffolder meets EMAS crew who saved him after 12 shocks
stories.body: A Northamptonshire scaffolder went into cardiac arrest at home and arrested again after prolonged CPR and 12 defibrillator shocks. His friend's CPR, guided by a call handler, bought vital time, and he has now met his lifesavers.
stories.why: Bystander CPR and call-handler support give crews a fighting chance.

stories.headline: NQP Graduate Guarantee petition passes 10,000
stories.body: A petition to extend the NHS Graduate Guarantee to newly qualified paramedics has passed 10,000 signatures, so the Government will now have to respond. It needs 100,000 to be considered for a debate in Parliament.
stories.why: Job security for NQPs affects every crew, from students now to the colleagues they will join.

stories.headline: Wrexham ambulance handovers average two and a half hours
stories.body: Handovers at Wrexham Maelor are far over Wales's 45-minute target. The Welsh Ambulance Service is using 'call before convey' and advanced paramedic practitioners treating people at home to keep ambulances on the road.
stories.why: Long handovers keep crews off the road, so alternatives to conveyance matter more than ever.

stories.headline: LAS shares recordings of sexual harassment of call staff
stories.body: London Ambulance Service released anonymised call extracts showing the abuse its control-room staff face. About a third of its 462 reported sexual abuse incidents were aimed at 999 and 111 colleagues.
stories.why: Abuse of control-room colleagues is abuse of the whole team, and it should always be reported.

stories.headline: NI Health Minister backs See and Treat and Hear and Treat
stories.body: On a visit to NIAS, Health Minister Robbie Butler highlighted that 44,064 incidents were resolved by See and Treat and 19,612 by Hear and Treat in 2025-26, keeping patients out of busy EDs.
stories.why: Care closer to home is now a core part of the job, not an add-on.

stories.headline: Heart stopped seven times: Kent man meets his team
stories.body: A 59-year-old man went into cardiac arrest seven times at home. Call handlers, a CFR, paramedics, AAPs and a critical care paramedic achieved sustained ROSC after nearly two hours, and he has now met the team.
stories.why: A powerful reminder that every link in the chain of survival counts.

stories.headline: EEAST reports its busiest year ever for 999 calls
stories.body: East of England Ambulance Service took nearly 100,000 calls in September and attended over 84,000 incidents. Crews lost more than 18,000 hours to hospital handover waits, and there have been over 1.2 million calls since September 2025.
stories.why: Every hour lost at a hospital door is a crew not free for the next 999 call.

stories.headline: Physicians warn corridor care needs whole-system fix
stories.body: The Royal College of Physicians welcomed the £140m urgent care boost but warned that around 2,400 corridor care cases happen in England’s emergency departments every day, with 92,177 in August.
stories.why: Crowded EDs mean longer handovers, so crews are held at hospital while calls wait in the community.

stories.headline: Five-year review of cardiac arrests in Northern Ireland
stories.body: NIAS and Queen’s University reviewed 14,255 out-of-hospital cardiac arrests from 2018 to 2022. Bystander CPR rose from 70% to 79%, but only 5% of patients were shocked with a public defib before the ambulance arrived.
stories.why: Bystander CPR is rising, but public defibs are still rarely used before crews get there.

stories.headline: NEAS staff trial an AI note-taking tool
stories.body: 38 North East Ambulance Service staff are testing a tool on their iPads that records and summarises patient conversations, in an eight-week trial. A clinician checks every note before it is added to the record, and the trust will decide next steps in November.
stories.why: Less time typing could mean more time with patients, but the clinician still owns the record.

stories.headline: NQP award honours paramedic who lifts colleagues
stories.body: SECAmb paramedic Matty Baker has won the Alice Clark Award, given in memory of a 21-year-old NQP who died in service in 2022. It recognises growth from newly qualified to experienced practitioner, and Matty was praised for his kindness and humour.
stories.why: The NQP years are about growth, and looking after each other on tough shifts matters.

stories.headline: £140m winter boost includes 40 extra EMAS ambulances
stories.body: The government is funding 14 urgent care schemes in England ahead of winter, including £6.35m for 40 more double-crewed ambulances at East Midlands Ambulance Service and £12m for a replacement ambulance hub in Shrewsbury.
stories.why: More crews on the road in the East Midlands this winter, though the money is spread across just 14 schemes.

stories.headline: Royal College of Paramedics holds first mental health conference
stories.body: The College’s inaugural mental health conference runs in Cheltenham on Tuesday 20 October and is open to students, with Simon Weston CBE giving the keynote and sessions on patient mental health care and paramedic wellbeing.
stories.why: Mental health is a growing part of the job, and of looking after ourselves. Watch for the talks being shared afterwards.

stories.headline: Aspiring paramedic, 15, helps save a man’s life
stories.body: A 15-year-old from Mansfield Woodhouse who had done a CPR course with EMAS started compressions on a 75-year-old man in cardiac arrest and kept going until crews arrived. He now runs free CPR sessions for young people.
stories.why: Bystander CPR is the link crews depend on. Community training is paying off, and a future colleague is already making a difference.

stories.headline: Cyclist backs CPR push after bystanders saved him
stories.body: A cyclist survived a roadside cardiac arrest near Brands Hatch after passers-by gave more than 20 minutes of CPR. KSS Air Ambulance ran public CPR and defibrillator sessions for Restart a Heart Day.
stories.why: Twenty minutes of bystander CPR bought the time crews needed. That is the case for public training in one story.
